---
title: Working with an Agent
llms-description: "What a coding agent supervising a Steward run decides, what it may never do, how its instructions ship with the package, and what to expect when you ask it how the run is going."
---

## Overview

Steward is built to be operated by a coding agent, and its own surface is shaped
for that: almost every verb is one an agent runs, while yours is `init`,
`signoff`, editing the definition and `_steward.md`, and asking questions in
prose.

An agent is **not** required. A timer guarantees the mechanical half of
supervision, so a run converges perfectly well with nobody in session — see
[the division of responsibility](index.qmd#who-does-what). What an agent adds is
judgement, and what its absence costs is judgement alone.

This page is about what that agent does, and what it may not. Its actual
operating instructions are a separate artifact you do not have to write: see
[The Agent Runbook](runbook.qmd).

## Its instructions ship with the package

``` bash
steward runbook
```

The runbook is a **command rather than a file**, and that is a deliberate
choice. Instructions and implementation ship together, so an agent can never
follow last year's runbook against this year's CLI. There is nothing in your
workspace to keep up to date, and nothing to copy into a prompt.

That divides cleanly from `_steward.md`:

|  | `steward runbook` | `_steward.md` |
|----|----|----|
| answers | how Steward works | what *this human* wants |
| owner | the package | you |
| lifetime | ships with the version | lives with the project |
| example | "call `tend` every ten minutes; never block on a human" | "sandbox timeouts in this eval are expected" |

`AGENTS.md`, written by `init`, is the thin bootstrap that points at both. It is
the only thing that has to be discovered by convention.

## What it decides

The agent's jobs are the ones that need judgement, which is to say the ones a
turn refuses to do:

|  |  | status |
|----|----|----|
| **tuner** | raise sample concurrency while the provider shows no pushback, and pull back when it does | not yet built |
| **grouper** | collapse many computed error classes into two or three questions you can actually answer | not yet built |
| **investigator** | judge scan results, which carry no verdict of their own | not yet built |
| **author** | write up what happened, per task, so the run leaves something a person can read | not yet built |

Today its live work is narrower: keep the run converging, read the attention
list, bring you what is yours, and dispose of what it has genuinely resolved.

## What it may never do

These are settled and binding now, and the runbook states them as flatly as
possible. No situation makes any of them correct.

-   **`steward signoff`.** It is a human attestation that the results are
    accepted. An agent running it is the one thing that would make the whole
    record meaningless.
-   **Edit the definition.** It is your statement of what is being measured, and
    afterwards an agent's edit is indistinguishable from yours. It reads it, runs
    it, and raises anything that looks wrong as a *question*. This includes
    adding a comment explaining what the eval set is for: an agent handed a
    definition was never told why it exists, and a plausible-but-invented
    rationale is worse than none, because a later reader cannot tell it from the
    author's.
-   **Write `_steward.md`.** It proposes; you write. Both halves.
-   **Move or delete a log.** Not even an empty cancelled one, and not into a
    folder named for discards. Resume matches logs where they are.
-   **Answer a tool approval or an `ask_user`.** A worker that has stopped for a
    human decision is asking whether the eval may *do* something, and answering
    is authority over what is being measured. The agent surfaces it, names the
    worker, prints the command that attaches to it, and waits.

::: {.callout-important}
None of these is enforced by access control, and Steward does not pretend
otherwise. `signoff` records who signed; the runbook says plainly that the agent
never signs. A forged signature is visible rather than prevented — the same
bargain a commit author line makes.
:::

## What it should ask about first

`steward ack` sits in an awkward place and is worth knowing about, because it is
the gate on the agent's own autonomy: acknowledging an item removes it from
`status.md`, from the turn's output, and from the verdict, so an agent free to
ack unasked can silence its own attention list.

So acking is **ask-first**, recorded as `--by human` with your reason. The one
exception is narrow: an item the agent investigated and resolved itself — a file
that turned out to be a partial upload, say — is its own disposal, recorded
`--by agent`. The test is whether anyone but the agent would have to know.

`steward raise` is the opposite case and needs no permission at all. It records
that a decision of yours is now in front of you, and it **closes nothing** — the
item stays in `status.md`, and the verdict still counts it. All it changes is
that the agent stops being handed work it has already done everything about
([Reading Status](status.qmd#raising-which-is-the-agents-half-of-the-same-thing)).

## Its own queue

``` bash
steward collect
```

This is the verb an agent starts a session with. It prints the same three
sections `status` does and adds the stretch of history since the agent last
looked — then records that it looked, which is what makes *nobody has read this
run in six hours* something Steward can report rather than something you have to
notice.

The two halves behave differently on purpose. **History** is a stream with a
cursor, so reading it advances a bookmark. **Decisions** are a set, and one
leaves the agent's queue only when the agent *acts* — `ack` to close it, `raise`
to hand it to you. Nothing is consumed by being looked at, so an agent whose
session dies mid-investigation finds its work waiting.

Anything the agent's view sets aside is **counted** rather than dropped: a
decisions section reading `Nothing for you. 2 raised, awaiting a person.` is
telling the agent there are two open decisions and neither is its to make. That
matters because an agent can read a label but cannot reason about what it was
never shown.

## When it should stop and ask you

Rather than working around: identity or resume errors, where the manifest and the
logs disagree about what the eval *is*; numbers that fail sanity; anything
requiring a destructive or irreversible action; persistent credential failures;
or a non-converging loop — the same task failing across three launches.

A stop is not a teardown. Healthy work keeps running, and the journal gets a
final entry with the state and a hypothesis.

## Three ways an agent can relate to a run

Because the timer guarantees the floor, attachment is a choice rather than an
obligation:

| posture | how it learns something happened | latency to judgement |
|----|----|----|
| **attached, reactive** | something watches the turn output or the journal and wakes it | seconds — worth setting up for a run being watched closely |
| **attached, periodic** | its own wake-ups; it may call `tend` directly to force a turn early | its own interval |
| **transient** | it reads accumulated state when it attaches, with `steward collect` | until somebody opens a session |

**The transient posture is the common one**, and it is the one to design your
expectations around: somebody opens a session in the morning, and the agent reads
what the night produced. That is why the workspace has to carry everything — the
journal records what each turn *observed*, not only what was decided, so a fresh
session can tell which problems are getting worse rather than inheriting a flat
list. `steward collect` is how it reads that, and how it knows where it stopped
last time.

Calling `tend` is still useful, but it means *give me a turn now* rather than
*keep this run alive*. An agent that has just resolved something should tend
immediately rather than wait out the interval.

## What to expect when you ask "how is it going"

The runbook is emphatic about this, and it is worth knowing so you can tell when
it is being followed:

> An agent asked for an update should run `steward status --format md` and render
> what it printed — every section, in order, in full.

Brevity is not the failure; **substitution** is. The detail *is* the answer, and
a summary replaces your judgement with the agent's at the exact moment you were
trying to form your own. Analysis is held by default and goes *below* the
snapshot, marked as the agent's, only when it is both important and not obvious
from the snapshot itself.

If you get a paragraph of reassurance instead of the table, the agent is not
following its runbook.

## Setting one up

There is nothing to configure. Point an agent at the workspace directory and it
finds `AGENTS.md`, which tells it to run `steward runbook` and read
`_steward.md`. Steward makes no assumption about which harness you use and
carries no harness-specific setup.

The one thing worth doing deliberately is the conversation at launch, because
**the cost of a question is not constant** — it decays with your availability.
Asked while you are present it costs a sentence; asked at 3am it stalls until
morning. So front-load the decisions you can predict, and write the answers into
`_steward.md` where they hold overnight ([Standing Rules](directives.qmd)).
